newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH CONSTITUTION READY FOR REFERENDUM.
newsitem.headline: POLISH CONSTITUTION READY FOR REFERENDUM.

text.p: Poland's parliament gave a final approval on Wednesday to a new constitution that would replace the communist-era charter eight years after the fall of the old regime.

The national assembly of both houses of parliament voted 451 to 40 with six abstentions to adopt the constitution, which guarantees civil and economic liberties and keeps the state and the powerful Roman Catholic church separated, after adopting most amendments proposed by President Aleksander Kwasniewski.

"This an exceptional and moving moment...a historic decision has been taken," Kwasniewski told deputies after they sang the national anthem. He said he would set the date of a nationwide referendum on the constitution for May 25.
If approved in the poll, the bill will take effect three months after the president signs it, replacing the obsolete Stalinist-era 1952 charter amended by many, often unclear interim laws.
"The constitution guarantees...legal order, democratic and effective government and strengthens independence of courts," said Kwasniewski.

The constitution, heatedly debated by two parliaments since 1992, has become a battleground before general elections, due around September, pitting the ruling coalition dominated by ex-communists against right-wing groups outside parliament.
The groups, including the powerful Solidarity Electoral Action (AWS), support their own constitution draft, which adheres to religious values and bans abortion.

They say the current parliament -- elected in 1993 and dominated by parties with communist roots, the Democtratic Left Alliance (SLD) and the Peasant Party (PSL) -- has no moral right to approve the constitution for the democratic Poland.
Solidarity, hoping to defeat the ex-communist the coming elections, is runnig neck-in-neck in opinion polls with the SLD, supported by between 20 and 30 percent depending on a survey.

The right wants Poles to choose in the referendum between its draft and the current charter but parliamentarians say this is not possible without amending the current laws on legislative procedures, for which there is no time.

The most radical opposition group, the Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland (ROP), has urged voters to reject the parliament-backed constitution. Solidarity still analyses the charter and is yet to instruct its supporters on how to vote.
A recent opinion poll by public CBOS agency showed that 41 percent of Poles would support parliament's constitution, 15 percent would reject it while the rest was undecided.
Many economists criticise the constitution for including too many social safety net provisions that pave the way for creating a welfare state, which the meagre national budget cannot afford.

The charter guarantees free publicly funded basic health care, free basic education for all Poles and a minimum wage. It obliges the government to act to curb unemployment and stimulate housing construction.
"Unrealistic promises of social security should not exist in the constitution," said Bohdan Wyznikiewicz, senior analyst at the Market Economy Research Institute (IBnGR).

But Wyznikiewicz and other analysts praised the constitution for capping the public debt at 60 percent of gross domestic product and forbiding the government to finance the budget deficit through the central bank.

The constitution would also slightly weaken the presidency, with parliament allowed to overthrow the president's veto by three-fifths of votes in the lower house rather than the present two-thirds majority.
The constitution bans fascist, communist and racist political parties.

The right-wingers say that leftist-dominated parliament and the president, also an ex-communist, have been hastily pushing the constitution through to stage the referendum before a visit by Pope John Paul ll starting on May 31.
The Polish-born pontif's trip might turn many voters against the passed secular-minded constitution, they say.
